title.en: A boy, a goat and some bells

text.en: Chinna loves his pet kid, a baby goat named Tara, and wants to buy her shiny tinkling bells for ten rupees. When he loses his money he is sad. Later, when a fruit seller gives him extra change by mistake, Chinna must decide what to do. In this chapter you will read the story, learn words for good qualities, compare with -er and -est, find opposite words, put events in order and think about what you would do in hard situations.

Chinna was a little boy in grade 4 who lived in a village, loved storybooks and had many friends. Most of all he loved his pet kid Tara. A kid is a young goat under six months, and Tara was five months old and milky white. On the way home from school he saw a pair of shiny tinkling bells at Chacha's shop and wanted them for Tara. They cost ten rupees. He put his hand in his pocket and found that the money Dadaji had given him was missing. He searched all his pockets, returned the bells and walked home sadly.
At home Chinna put his shoes in the corner, dropped his bag, and rested his head on the table. His mother Kamala saw this, came to him and asked gently what had happened. Chinna hugged her and cried, then told her about the missing money. Kamala consoled him, said she would give him money for the bells, and asked him to be careful with money in the future. She then took him to the market to buy fruits and vegetables.
At the pineapple stall the fruit seller said each pineapple cost forty-five rupees. Kamala bought two and gave a hundred-rupee note. She asked Chinna to take the change while she went to other shops. The fruit seller gave Chinna two ten-rupee notes, which was ten rupees too much, by mistake. Chinna ran to his mother with a mischievous smile and asked if he could buy the bells and chocolates with the extra money. Kamala said that this was stealing, and asked him how he had felt when his own money was missing. Chinna said he had felt sad and angry, and Kamala said the fruit seller would feel the same.
Chinna thought about it and ran back to return the extra money. The fruit seller was very happy and called Chinna an honest boy. Kamala was pleased and took Chinna to Chacha's shop, just as Chacha was about to close. Chinna paid ten rupees for the bells, tied them round Tara's neck, and Tara came running when she heard them tinkle. The story teaches us that being honest is right, and that we should think how others feel.
Calm, honest, loyal, kind, fair, truth, respect, courage, love and peace are words for good qualities and values. Honest means telling the truth and not taking what is not yours. Loyal means staying true to friends or family. Courage means being brave when something is difficult or scary. Fair means treating everyone equally.
Adjectives are words that tell about people and things, like tall and small. When we compare two people or things, we add -er and use than. Charu is taller than Chinna. An ant is smaller than an elephant. When we compare more than two, we add -est. Jasmine is the tallest in the group. February is the shortest month. So: tall, taller, tallest; small, smaller, smallest; fast, faster, fastest; cold, colder, coldest.
Beautiful has the opposite ugly. Reward has the opposite punishment. Buy has the opposite sell. Whispered has the opposite shouted. To retell a story in order: Chinna wanted bells, found his money missing, hugged his mother, went to the market, returned the extra money, and finally bought the bells. Sequencing a story means putting the events in the order they happened.

If friends ask you to show them your answers, kindly say no, because copying is not fair, and offer to study together. If you see someone take something without asking, you should tell a trusted adult. If a classmate has no snack, you can share, because sharing makes both of you happy.

problem.en: Fill in -er or -est: Jay was the fast___ person in the race.

text.en: The race has many people, so it is a whole group.
We add -est to fast.
So: Jay was the fastest person in the race.

why.en: For two people we would write faster than.

text.en: Beautiful means very nice to look at.

why.en: We need a word with the opposite meaning.

text.en: The opposite is ugly.

why.en: Ugly means not nice to look at.

problem.en: Order the events: A. Chinna returned the extra money. B. Chinna lost his money. C. Chinna tied the bells on Tara.

text.en: First Chinna lost his money: B.
Then he returned the extra money: A.
At last he tied the bells on Tara: C. The order is B, A, C.

why.en: The ending shows the happy result.

prompt.en: Tell the story of Chinna and explain why returning the money was right.

requiredIdeas.en: Chinna lost his money and was sad
The fruit seller gave extra change
Chinna remembered how he had felt
He returned it and was called honest

points.en: Chinna wanted tinkling bells for his pet kid Tara.
He returned the extra money because he knew how it felt to lose money.
Honest, kind, fair and loyal are words for good qualities.
Use -er with than for two things and -est for more than two.
Opposites have opposite meanings: buy and sell, beautiful and ugly.
